topics.title: Thailand-Cambodia
bullets: Recently, fighting along the Thailand–Cambodia border has escalated into a high-intensity military confrontation.
The clashes have displaced over 800,000 civilians from border regions.
Dozens of casualties have been reported on both sides. History of Thailand Cambodia dispute –
Preah Vihear temple, built in the 11th–12th centuries, reflects the Hindu-Buddhist heritage of the Khmer Empire, which once ruled much of present-day Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, and Vietnam.

Though built by the Khmer (ancestors of modern Cambodians), the area of Preah Vihear has historically been under the control of both Khmer and Siamese (Thai) kingdoms, due to shifting boundaries over centuries.
In 1431, Siamese forces sacked Angkor Thom, forcing the Khmer king to relocate his capital southward; over the next 400 years, Siam steadily encroached on Cambodian territory.
By 1794, a weakened Khmer monarch ceded control of northwestern Cambodia (including areas near Preah Vihear) to Siam.
In 1863, Cambodian King Norodom invited France to make Cambodia a protectorate, aiming to escape Siamese dominance.
In 1867, Siam renounced suzerainty over Cambodia in exchange for territorial concessions, including the area around Preah Vihear.
The 1904 Franco-Siamese treaty defined the border as running along the Dangrek Mountains watershed, which technically placed Preah Vihear on Siamese (Thai) territory.

In 1907, French colonial officials drew a topographic map that deviated from the watershed and placed Preah Vihear in Cambodian territory; Siamese representatives did not protest or offer a counter- map.
During World War II (1941), Thailand seized Preah Vihear in alliance with Japan but returned it to French Indochina after the war.
In 1954, after France withdrew from Indochina, Thai troops occupied Preah Vihear again, prompting Cambodia to file a case at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 1959.
Thailand argued the 1907 map was not valid and claimed accessibility from Thai side showed its sovereignty, while Cambodia argued Thailand had accepted the map for decades.
In 1962, the ICJ ruled 9–3 in favor of Cambodia, citing Thailand's acquiescence to the map and ordering Thai troops to withdraw and return relics.
Cambodia’s Prince Sihanouk took symbolic steps toward peace and reconciliation, allowing Thais to visit Preah Vihear without visas and letting Thailand keep the relics, though tensions persisted.
From the 1970s to 1990s, the temple was inaccessible due to Khmer Rouge insurgency and landmines; both sides refrained from asserting tourist or military presence.
In 2008, Cambodia applied to list Preah Vihear as a UNESCO World Heritage Site; Thailand opposed the move, saying it implied Cambodian control over disputed surrounding land (4.6 sq. km).

The issue inflamed Thai domestic politics, with the opposition PAD (“yellow shirts”) accusing Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej of compromising sovereignty, while Cambodia’s Hun Sen used the issue to boost nationalist support.

After UNESCO approved Cambodia’s application on July 8, 2008, tensions escalated: military buildups, border skirmishes, political resignations, and diplomatic standoffs followed; the area saw armed clashes, notably in 2009, causing casualties.
Attempts at peaceful resolution failed, as Thai PM Abhisit Vejjajiva rejected mediation and Cambodia refused to extradite ex-Thai PM Thaksin, instead appointing him an advisor, worsening ties.
Meanwhile, locals suffered economically, and the dispute remains partially unresolved, especially regarding the surrounding land. Three sites at the centre of dispute –

Prasat Ta Muen is a Mahayana Buddhist religious site, constructed as a dharamshala (resting place for travellers) and one of the 18 such sites built by King Jayavarman VII. ➢The structure is made of laterite (reddish clay-like material) and resembles a single, tall, tower-like spire.

Prasat Ta Muen Tot, located 340 metres from Prasat Ta Muen, was built in the 13th century and is one of the 102 hospitals or shrines commissioned by King Jayavarman VII. ➢It features a principal square Prasat with a front porch made of sandstone and laterite. ➢A library stands to the right of the Prasat, surrounded by laterite walls and a southeastern arch (gopura). ➢The gopura has a Khmer inscription in Sanskrit ordered by King Jayavarman VII, paying tribute to Phra Phaisachaya Khuru Waituraya (Bodhisattva of pharmacology) and detailing the roles of doctors and caregivers. ➢The main inscription is preserved at the National Library, Tha Wasukri, Bangkok.

Prasat Ta Muen Thom is the main and oldest structure, built as a Hindu shrine dedicated to Lord Shiva in the 12th century by King Udayadityavarman II, and is central to the Thai-Cambodian conflict. What is happening currently?

Tensions reignited on December 8, 2025, after a Thai soldier was killed in cross-border firing in Ubon Ratchathani; Thailand blamed Cambodian fire, while Cambodia accused Thai forces of initiating the attack in Preah Vihear province.
Since December 10, 2025, the conflict has escalated into high- intensity military operations, marking a breakdown in international mediation efforts.

On December 10, the Royal Thai Army launched Operation Sattawat, leading to ground and air escalation and the seizure of multiple localities and command posts in northern Cambodia, including areas around Chong An Ma.
By December 11, the Royal Thai Air Force carried out airstrikes up to 90 km inside Cambodian territory, hitting targets in Siem Reap province, near the Angkor Wat region.
Cambodia retaliated with BM-21 Grad rocket barrages, striking civilian areas in Thai provinces of Sisaket, Surin, and Buriram.
Between December 11 and 17, mass displacement surged, with over 800,000 civilians displaced across both countries.
Since fighting resumed on December 8, at least 50 people have been killed, including the first reported Thai civilian deaths on December 11.

Cambodia has accused Thailand of using “toxic smoke” and targeting civilian infrastructure such as schools and displacement camps, while Thailand alleges Cambodia is using civilians as human shields by placing rocket systems in populated areas.
On December 12, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that a ceasefire was “back” after speaking to both sides, but confusion followed.
On December 13, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul denied any agreed truce, stating operations would continue until there was “no more harm or threat” to Thai territory.

As of December 16–17, Thailand has demanded that Cambodia declare a unilateral ceasefire first, while Cambodia maintains its actions are defensive and has urged intervention by the UN Security Council.

Amid the escalation, Thailand’s Cabinet approved 2.44 billion baht from the central fund (FY 2026) to reinforce the military and strengthen border security along the Thai–Cambodia border. Other disputes between the countries –
The conflict is not limited to territorial claims; it is rooted in centuries of historical rivalry between two once-powerful empires—Siam (Thailand) and the Khmer Empire (Cambodia).

This cultural and historical rivalry has been amplified in modern times by Cambodia’s slower development, which suffered under French colonialism and the devastating rule of the Khmer Rouge in the 1970s.
Cambodians often feel looked down upon by Thailand, and resentment persists over perceived Thai superiority and domination in regional affairs.
In return, Thai conservatives accuse Cambodia of internationalizing disputes and provoking tensions for domestic political gain.

The two nations have even clashed over cultural heritage, with disputes involving traditional clothing, masked dance forms, cuisine, and boxing styles—each accusing the other of cultural appropriation.
These cultural disputes have further fueled popular animosity, especially on social media, making rational dialogue between the governments even more difficult.

topics.title: New Ramsar Sites
bullets: Recently, Siliserh Lake (Rajasthan) and Kopra Jalashay (Chhattisgarh) have been added to the Ramsar List of Wetlands of International Importance.
With this inclusion, India’s total Ramsar sites have increased to 96.
The recognition strengthens wetland conservation, biodiversity protection, and sustainable management across the country. What are Ramsar sites?
Wetlands are areas where water either covers the soil or is present near the soil surface throughout the year or for varying durations, including the growing season.

The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands defines wetlands as ➢ “areas of marsh, fen, peat land or water, whether natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt, including areas of marine water the depth of which at low tide does not exceed six meters”.

For the purposes of this classification, wetlands must have one or more of the following three attributes: (1) at least periodically, the land supports predominantly hydrophytes; (2) the substrate is predominantly undrained hydric soil; and (3) the substrate is non-soil and is saturated with water or covered by shallow water at some time during the growing season of each year”.
The Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, also known as the Convention on Wetlands, is an intergovernmental treaty for the conservation and wise use of wetlands.
A Ramsar Site is a wetland site designated to be of international importance.
These wetlands are protected under strict guidelines of the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands.
The Convention was adopted in the Iranian city of Ramsar in 1971 and came into force in 1975.
Since then, almost 90% of UN member states, from all the world’s geographic regions, have acceded to become “Contracting Parties”.
This requires international cooperation, policy making, capacity building and technology transfer.
The Contracting Parties meet every three years at a Conference of the Contracting Parties (COP) to discuss policy issues.
They report on the activities of the previous three years through National Reports.
The next Conference of the Contracting Parties (COP15) will be held in Victoria Falls, Zimbabwe in July 2025.
The Montreux Record is a register of wetland sites on the List of Wetlands of International Importance and is maintained under Ramsar sited.
It includes sites where changes in ecological character have occurred, are occurring, or are likely to occur as a result of human interference.
The Montreux Record was established by Recommendation 4.8 of the Conference of the Contracting Parties (1990).
Today, the Ramsar List is the world’s largest network of protected areas.
There are over 2,400 Ramsar Sites on the territories of 172 Convention Contracting Parties across the world, covering more than 2.5 million square kilometres.
The world’s first Site was the Cobourg Peninsula in Australia, designated in 1974.
The largest Sites are Rio Negro in Brazil (120,000 square kilometres), and Ngiri-Tumba-Maindombe in Congo.
The countries with the most Sites are the United Kingdom with 175 and Mexico with 144.

Bolivia has the largest area with 148,000 square km under the Convention protection; Canada, Chad, Congo and the Russian Federation have also each designated over 100,000 square km. Ramsar convention in India –
India is a party to the Convention since 1982 and India was a member of the Standing Committee from 1999-2002.
As of Dec 24, 2025, India has 96 Ramsar sites.
Chilika Lake in Orissa and Keoladeo National Park in Rajasthan were recognised as the first Ramsar sites in 1981 in India.
Globally, wetlands cover 6.4 per cent of the geographical area of the world.
As of 2025, with 91 wetlands, Indian wetlands cover a total of approx 15.2 million hectares of land. The total number of wetlands is 7,57,060.
Of the 15.2 million hectares , inland-natural wetlands account for 45% and coastal-natural wetlands 25%.
India has 19 types of wetlands.
Gujarat's wetland area covers maximum area about 17.56% of the state's geographical area and 23.14% of the total wetland area in India.
Tamil Nadu continues to have maximum number of Ramsar Sites (20 sites) followed by Uttar Pradesh (10 sites). Awards -
The Ramsar Wetland Conservation Awards were established in 1996 to recognize individuals and organizations for wetland conservation and wise use.
The awards were created at the 6th Conference of the Parties (COP6) in 1996 through Resolution VI.18.
Recipients receive the Evian Special Prize of USD 10,000, sponsored by Danone.
The awards have been presented six times during Ramsar COP meetings in 1999, 2002, 2005, 2008, 2012, and 2015.
There are three award categories: ➢Wetland Wise Use ➢Wetland Innovation ➢Young Wetland Champions
The Ramsar Wetland Conservation Award for Innovation recognizes a person, project, program, or policy that has used an innovative technique or approach for wetland conservation.
The Ramsar Wetland Conservation Award for Young Wetland Champions honors individuals or groups aged 18- 30 for their work in wetland conservation, wise use, and restoration.

The Ramsar Wetland Indigenous Peoples Conservation and Wise Use Award acknowledges groups or individuals for leadership and transformative projects involving indigenous peoples in wetland conservation. New sites – Siliserh Lake –
Siliserh Lake in Alwar district, Rajasthan has been designated as a Ramsar site, becoming India’s 96th wetland of international importance.
The recognition was announced by the Convention on Wetlands, reflecting India’s growing focus on conserving ecologically significant water bodies.
Along with Siliserh Lake, the Kopra Reservoir in Bilaspur district, Chhattisgarh, has also been added to the global Ramsar list.
Siliserh Lake supports over 100 species of birds and animals, including migratory birds such as cranes and resident species like kingfishers.
The lake serves as a crucial habitat and feeding ground, making it a popular spot for birdwatchers and nature enthusiasts.
Its proximity to the Sariska Tiger Reserve enhances its ecological importance within the Aravalli landscape.
Siliserh Lake was constructed in 1845 by Maharaja Vinay Singh to supply drinking water to Alwar city.
Historic aqueduct remnants around the lake highlight its engineering and heritage significance. Kopra Reservoir –
Kopra Reservoir is located in Baloda Bazar–Bhatapara district, Chhattisgarh, in an agriculture-dominated region with seasonal rivers.
Constructed in 1993 as an irrigation and water storage project, it has gradually developed into a natural freshwater wetland.
The reservoir lies in the upper catchment of the Mahanadi River, is primarily rain-fed, and supported by seasonal streams.
Kopra acts as a key ecological buffer, absorbing excess monsoon rainwater, reducing floods, and mitigating drought impacts.
It supports over 149–161 bird species, with seasonal populations exceeding 20,000 birds during peak periods.

Resident species: Around 103 species depend on the wetland year-round. ➢Migratory species: About 58–60 species, including Bar- headed Goose, Common Pochard, and River Tern, use it as a winter stopover. ➢Threatened birds recorded include the Endangered Egyptian Vulture, Vulnerable Greater Spotted Eagle, etc.
The reservoir supports local livelihoods by providing drinking water, sustaining fisheries, and irrigating fertile agricultural land.
Kopra Reservoir was officially designated a Ramsar Site on December 12, 2025, becoming Chhattisgarh’s first Ramsar wetland.
It is also India’s 96th Ramsar Site, designated alongside Siliserh Lake (Rajasthan).
The designation promotes eco-tourism and birdwatching, creating local employment opportunities. Also, it encourages community participation in conservation and sustainable livelihood practices.
The recognition aligns with the “Chhattisgarh Anjor Vision 2047”, which aims to secure Ramsar status for 20 wetlands by 2030.

The wetland is located at approximately 22°4′N, 82°2′E, about 13 km east of Bilaspur city. Best time to visit: November to February, ideal for migratory bird sightings; entry is generally free for the public. . Indian Initiatives -
Protecting existing wetlands and restoring degraded ones is critical for building climate resilience and ensuring our survival.
While Ramsar sites are prioritised for protection, there are several other urban wetlands which must also be accorded due importance.
At the national level, the MoEFCC also implements several programs and initiatives aimed at conserving and managing wetlands in the country.
The National Wetland Conservation Program (NWCP) launched in 1985 provides financial and technical assistance to states and UTs for the preservation and management of wetlands.
The National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) was approved by Government of India as 100% centrally sponsored scheme.
To enhance synergy and prevent overlap, the two schemes were consolidated into a centrally sponsored scheme called the 'National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Eco-systems' (NPCA) in February 2013.
The MoEF&CC has notified Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017, under the provisions of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
These rules serve as a regulatory framework for the conservation and management of wetlands across the country.
The aim is to conserve, manage, and maintain the ecological character of the wetlands without restricting their wise use.
The Government of India also launched the Amrit Sarovar Mission in 2022.
Under the Mission, 75 water bodies will be developed and rejuvenated in each district of the country as a part of the celebration of Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav.
In total, the Mission aims at creating 50,000 water bodies of a size of about an Acre or more.
The Amrit Dharohar initiative, part of the 2023-24 budget announcement, was launched by MoEF&CC in June 2023.
The initiative aims to promote Ramsar Sites' unique conservation values in the country, creating employment opportunities and supporting local livelihoods.
Implemented over three years, this initiative involves collaboration with Central Government ministries, State Wetland Authorities, and a network of institutions and individuals.
World Wetlands Day is celebrated every year on 2 February to mark the date of the adoption of the Ramsar Convention.
The Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change (MoEF&CC) in collaboration with Madhya Pradesh, organised a national event at Sirpur Lake, Indore to celebrate WWD 2024.
